idiom_name: compiler-enforced access levels with a private stored resource and one mediating method
implementation_notes: Swift's access control is compiler-enforced and finer than most: private limits an entity to its enclosing declaration and same-file extensions, fileprivate to the source file, internal is the default within a module, and package access spans the modules of one package - so the monitor can be a type whose stored resource is private and whose only exported path is a method that consults the policy, with private(set) for values that may be read but not written. The guarantee stops at the language's edges: classes are reference types shared freely, structs are copied out of the monitor as unmediated values, @testable import grants test targets access to internal entities by design, and NSObject subclasses stay reachable through the Objective-C runtime. On Apple platforms the tamperproof monitor is the system one - the App Sandbox limits the app's access to files, network and devices through entitlements that the app's own code cannot widen.
pitfalls: fileprivate and same-file extensions widen the monitor to the whole file, and internal - the default - to the whole module: only private is confined to the declaration, so keep mediated state in the type that decides.

Value semantics leak: a struct returned from a permitted read is an unmediated copy the monitor can never revoke, and Key-Value Coding on NSObject subclasses (setValue(_:forKey:)) bypasses access levels at runtime.
@testable import makes internal declarations visible to test targets - an intentional widening that must not be the only thing standing between the tests and the policy.

The Objective-C runtime reaches Swift classes through their dynamic dispatch table (@objc exposure, swizzling, class replacement); where the boundary matters, keep mediated types out of ObjC-visible APIs and rely on the App Sandbox and entitlements for enforcement.
